description: Defining aerobic and anaerobic exercise and applying examples by intensity and duration.
content_html:
Two Ways Your Body Produces Energy

All physical activity requires energy, and the body produces that energy by breaking down glucose. The critical difference between the two energy pathways is whether sufficient oxygen is available. Aerobic exercise occurs when there is enough oxygen to fully break down glucose. The chemical summary is: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water. This process is efficient, releasing large amounts of energy, and can be sustained for a long time — making it the dominant pathway for moderate-intensity, longer-duration activities such as a 10 km run, a long swim or a cycling time trial.

Anaerobic exercise occurs when the intensity of effort is so high that the cardiovascular system cannot deliver oxygen to the muscles fast enough. The body bypasses oxygen entirely and breaks down glucose without it: glucose → energy + lactic acid. This pathway is fast but inefficient — it produces far less energy per glucose molecule and cannot be sustained for long because lactic acid accumulates in the muscles, causing fatigue and the familiar burning sensation. Sprinting 100 m, an explosive plyometric jump or a short all-out rowing effort are classic examples of anaerobic activity.

Key Fact

Aerobic: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water. Anaerobic: glucose → energy + lactic acid. The key distinction is the presence or absence of sufficient oxygen — not simply whether the sport involves running or swimming.

Identifying Aerobic and Anaerobic Activity: Duration and Intensity

A common error is simply labelling a sport as “aerobic” or “anaerobic” without justifying the classification. The correct approach is to consider both the duration and the intensity of the effort. High-intensity activity lasting fewer than roughly ten seconds is almost entirely anaerobic because the demand for energy outpaces oxygen delivery. Activities lasting several minutes at moderate intensity are primarily aerobic. Many sports — such as football, netball and rugby — involve both pathways at different moments: a striker’s burst of speed to latch onto a through ball is anaerobic, but the sustained movement across the pitch throughout the match is predominantly aerobic.

Students often believe “aerobic” simply means easy or low-intensity exercise. This is incorrect. A trained 5,000 m runner racing at full competitive pace is still working aerobically — the intensity is high, but oxygen delivery keeps pace with demand throughout the race (approximately 13 minutes in duration). The correct justification is always intensity-and-duration together: “This activity is aerobic because the intensity, although high, can be maintained with sufficient oxygen delivery over the multi-minute duration.” Similarly, a short, explosive effort is anaerobic because the intensity is so extreme that oxygen cannot be delivered quickly enough — not because the activity is “hard” in some vague sense. Always frame your answer with both criteria.

Lactic Acid: Cause and Consequence

Lactic acid is produced whenever anaerobic respiration takes place — that is, whenever exercise intensity rises to the point where oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough. As lactic acid accumulates in the muscle fibres and bloodstream, it interferes with the chemical processes of muscle contraction and the athlete experiences the characteristic burning sensation and muscular fatigue. This is why anaerobic efforts cannot be sustained: a 100 m sprinter running at maximum effort will notice the burning onset in their legs in the final 20–30 metres of the race, and performance suffers unless the athlete eases off.

In many sports, the ability to tolerate or delay lactic acid accumulation is a key determinant of performance. A 400 m runner, for example, runs at an intensity that is predominantly anaerobic for approximately 45–50 seconds. Managing lactic acid accumulation through training — specifically by repeatedly stressing the anaerobic system in intervals — is a central goal of sprint conditioning programmes.

Many team sports require athletes to switch between aerobic and anaerobic energy systems within the same performance. In a game of basketball, a player spends much of the match jogging and walking (aerobic), but executes repeated explosive sprints, jumps and changes of direction (anaerobic). The same applies to a hockey winger or a rugby union flanker. When asked to classify the dominant energy system for a sport like this, consider what the athlete spends the most time doing, and what the critical performance moments demand. A basketball player’s overall fitness is predominantly aerobic; their game-deciding moments are predominantly anaerobic. Both systems must be trained.

Key Fact

Always justify aerobic/anaerobic classification using both intensity and duration. Aerobic examples: marathon running (moderate-high intensity, 2+ hours), 1,500 m swim (sustained effort over several minutes). Anaerobic examples: 100 m sprint (maximal intensity, ~10 seconds), shot-put throw (single explosive effort, under 3 seconds).
exam_tip_html: For “identify” and shorter questions on aerobic vs anaerobic, a common error is giving the activity name without any justification. Even a 1-mark question may expect you to say why: “anaerobic, because the high intensity means oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough.” For the 8-mark “Evaluate” question, students often produce one-sided answers that only describe the positive features of aerobic exercise without considering trade-offs, or vice versa. OCR’s levels-based mark scheme rewards (a) range of points, (b) a balanced argument, and (c) consistent sporting application. Build your response using a “For X… However Y…” structure, anchor each point to a named sport or athlete type, and end with a justified conclusion. Also note: OCR does not require you to define or use the terms EPOC, oxygen debt or DOMS at this level — focus on the definitions, word equations and the intensity-duration justification.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Aerobic exercise uses oxygen to break down glucose fully (producing CO⊂2; and water); anaerobic exercise occurs without sufficient oxygen and produces lactic acid as a by-product. Justify each classification with both intensity and duration evidence.
  • Lactic acid accumulates during anaerobic exercise, causing fatigue and the burning sensation in muscles. Activities lasting under approximately 10 seconds at maximal intensity are predominantly anaerobic; sustained moderate-to-high intensity effort is predominantly aerobic.
  • Many sports use both systems: explosive moments (anaerobic) sit alongside sustained movement (aerobic). A complete athlete trains both energy pathways.

practice_questions.text: Identify whether the following activity is aerobic or anaerobic: a swimmer completing a 200 m race at maximum effort in approximately 2 minutes.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: anaerobic (or predominantly anaerobic). The very high intensity over approximately 2 minutes means oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough. Accept: anaerobic exercise / uses the anaerobic pathway. Do not accept 'aerobic' for full credit.
1 mark for identifying that anaerobic exercise takes place without sufficient oxygen; 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down to produce energy and lactic acid as a by-product.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between aerobic and anaerobic exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct differences: aerobic uses oxygen / anaerobic does not use sufficient oxygen; aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water / anaerobic produces lactic acid; aerobic can be sustained for longer / anaerobic is short duration; aerobic is lower intensity / anaerobic is very high intensity. Do not award two marks for the same physiological point expressed differently.

practice_questions.text: A county-level basketball player performs a 30-second burst of high-intensity court sprints and jumps during a training drill. Describe why lactic acid accumulates during this effort and what effect this has on the player.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that the exercise intensity is too high for oxygen to be delivered fast enough, triggering anaerobic respiration; 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down without oxygen, producing lactic acid as a by-product; 1 mark for describing the consequence (lactic acid accumulates in the muscles and blood, causing fatigue and a burning sensation, limiting the player's ability to sustain the effort).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a 100 m sprinter and a 5,000 m runner require training for different energy systems, even though both are performing running events.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining that the 100 m sprint (approximately 10 seconds at maximal intensity) is predominantly anaerobic because the energy demand rate exceeds oxygen delivery capacity; 1 mark for stating the word equation for anaerobic respiration (glucose → energy + lactic acid); 1 mark for explaining that the 5,000 m (13+ minutes at sustained high intensity) is predominantly aerobic because oxygen delivery can keep pace with demand over the longer duration; 1 mark for stating the word equation for aerobic respiration (glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + water) and linking to the sustained effort the aerobic system allows.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level hockey player competes in a 70-minute outdoor match. Evaluate which energy system — aerobic or anaerobic — is more important to her overall match performance, and how each contributes at different points in the game.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Balanced, well-developed evaluation with consistent sporting application to hockey. Aerobic system: dominant during the majority of the match (jogging, sustained running, sustained press); defined correctly (glucose + oxygen → energy + CO2 + water); advantages — sustainable over 70 minutes, efficient energy production, supports cardiovascular endurance; supported by specific examples (maintaining pressing throughout the second half). Anaerobic system: dominant during explosive moments (sprinting to intercept a pass, penalty corner execution, tackling); defined correctly (glucose → energy + lactic acid); advantages — fast energy release for high-intensity bursts; limitations — lactic acid builds up, causes fatigue, cannot be sustained. Evaluation reaches a justified conclusion: aerobic system is more important overall due to the 70-minute duration, but anaerobic capacity determines performance in decisive moments. Both sides consistently anchored to hockey-specific examples.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both systems addressed with reasonable accuracy and applied to hockey; evaluation of both sides present; conclusion reached; some minor inaccuracies or undeveloped points.

Developing (3-4 marks): One system covered well, or both described with limited evaluation; sporting context present but limited; may not reach a clear conclusion.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic identification of aerobic or anaerobic with minimal development; little or no sporting application to hockey.

knowledge_checks.q: What is produced as a by-product of anaerobic exercise that causes muscle fatigue?
Which of the following correctly describes aerobic exercise?
options: Exercise using oxygen to break down glucose, producing energy, CO2 and water
Exercise that always produces lactic acid
Any exercise that makes you breathe faster

knowledge_checks.q: Aerobic respiration can be summarised as: glucose + oxygen → energy + carbon dioxide + _____.
When classifying exercise as aerobic or anaerobic, you must always consider both _____ and duration.
Match each activity to the energy system that dominates:
right: Mainly anaerobic — high intensity over short-medium duration

flashcard_questions.q: Complete the word equation: aerobic exercise — glucose + oxygen →
Complete the word equation: anaerobic exercise — glucose →

flashcard_questions.a: Exercise in the presence of sufficient oxygen, breaking down glucose fully to produce energy, CO2 and water.
Exercise in the absence of enough oxygen, producing lactic acid as a by-product.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does lactic acid cause fatigue in muscles?
flashcard_questions.a: It accumulates in the muscles and blood, impairing contraction and causing a burning sensation.

flashcard_questions.q: When classifying an activity as aerobic or anaerobic, what two factors must you always consider?
flashcard_questions.a: Both the duration and intensity of the effort.

flashcard_questions.q: A 100 m sprint lasts approximately 10 seconds at maximum intensity. Which energy pathway dominates?
flashcard_questions.a: Anaerobic — intensity is too high for oxygen delivery to keep pace.

flashcard_questions.q: A 1,500 m swim takes approximately 18 minutes. Which energy pathway dominates?
flashcard_questions.a: Aerobic — sufficient oxygen can be delivered over the sustained duration.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can anaerobic exercise not be sustained for long periods?
flashcard_questions.a: Lactic acid accumulates, causing muscular fatigue and a burning sensation that limits performance.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example each of aerobic and anaerobic activity in football.
flashcard_questions.a: Aerobic: sustained jogging across the pitch throughout the match. Anaerobic: a striker's explosive sprint to reach a through ball.

glossary_terms.definition: A simple sugar that is the body's primary fuel for energy production; broken down in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
Exercise that takes place in the presence of adequate oxygen, using glucose and oxygen to produce energy, carbon dioxide and water.
Exercise that takes place without sufficient oxygen, using glucose alone to produce energy and lactic acid as a by-product.
A waste product produced during anaerobic respiration that accumulates in the muscles and blood, causing fatigue and a burning sensation.
The level of effort or exertion applied during physical activity; a key factor in determining which energy system is used.
The length of time an activity is performed; alongside intensity, it determines whether aerobic or anaerobic pathways dominate.

hero_image_caption: Whether exercise is aerobic or anaerobic depends on its intensity and duration.
